C005.subject: Free trade policies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies export-oriented sectors in developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of firm-level productivity in East Asian export-oriented industries (e.g., electronics in South Korea, 1990-2010) using trade liberalization indices and R&D expenditure as controls. — Directly tests whether tariff reductions and export expansion correlate with faster technology adoption and innovation in targeted sectors, controlling for confounding factors like foreign direct investment.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of Latin American export sectors (e.g., automotive in Mexico vs. agricultural in Chile) under free trade agreements, drawing on World Bank and UNCTAD reports on technology transfer and patent filings. — Provides qualitative and quantitative evidence across different regional contexts, helping to assess whether the effect is robust or contingent on institutional factors.

[PATH:theoretical] Literature review of endogenous growth models incorporating trade openness and sectoral innovation (e.g., Aghion & Howitt, 1998; Grossman & Helpman, 1991) with extensions to developing economies. — Clarifies the mechanisms (e.g., learning-by-exporting, competitive pressure) that could accelerate or hinder technological advancement, guiding empirical predictions and causal interpretation.

qualifier.geographic: developing economies in East Asia and Latin America

C006.subject: Free trade policies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies export-oriented sectors in developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank's World Development Indicators and Enterprise Surveys for Southeast Asian and Sub-Saharan African economies (2000-2020) — Provides firm-level and macroeconomic data on export sector performance, trade liberalization timing, and employment/wage trends to test whether free trade policies correlate with detrimental outcomes in export-oriented industries.

[PATH:theoretical] Rodrik, D. (2018). 'Straight Talk on Trade: Ideas for a Sane World Economy'. Princeton University Press. — Offers a theoretical framework analyzing how trade liberalization can harm specific sectors in developing economies due to institutional weaknesses, labor market rigidities, and adjustment costs, directly relevant to the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of case studies on trade liberalization in Vietnam and Ghana (post-2000) by the Overseas Development Institute (ODI) — Synthesizes empirical evidence from two representative economies in the specified regions, allowing assessment of whether detrimental effects are common or context-dependent, and whether the hypothesis holds under different institutional conditions.

qualifier.geographic: Southeast Asian and Sub-Saharan African economies

C007.subject: Free trade policies
C007.object: domestic infant industries in developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies domestic infant industries in developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) for East Asian and Sub-Saharan African manufacturing firms (2000-2020) — Provides firm-level data on innovation inputs (R&D spending, new product introductions) and trade policy exposure (tariff rates, export/import ratios), enabling direct econometric testing of whether trade liberalization correlates with increased innovation in domestic infant industries in the specified regions and time period.

[PATH:literature] Case studies of infant industry development under trade liberalization in Vietnam and Ethiopia (post-2000) — These two countries represent contrasting outcomes in East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. Detailed qualitative and quantitative case studies (e.g., from Journal of International Economics or World Development) can reveal causal mechanisms—such as technology transfer, competitive pressure, or market access—that either confirm or refute the hypothesis, while controlling for institutional and policy differences.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of endogenous growth and trade with learning-by-doing (e.g., Young 1991, Aghion & Howitt 1998) applied to developing economies — Offers a framework to predict conditions under which free trade spurs or stifles innovation in infant industries (e.g., when domestic firms have sufficient absorptive capacity or face import competition). Testing these predictions against empirical patterns from the selected regions can help resolve the disputed status of the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: select developing economies in East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa

C008.subject: Free trade policies
C008.object: domestic infant industries in developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies domestic infant industries in developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative firm-level panel data from manufacturing censuses in Vietnam (1990s-2010s) and Kenya (1990s-2010s) analyzing productivity growth and market exit rates of infant industries before and after tariff reductions — Directly tests the causal impact of trade liberalization on domestic infant industry competitiveness using micro-level data, controlling for selection bias and industry heterogeneity.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of studies on 'learning-by-exporting' and 'import competition effects' in Southeast Asian and Sub-Saharan African economies during the 1990s-2010s, including meta-analysis of elasticity estimates — Synthesizes existing econometric evidence across multiple contexts to assess whether the net effect on infant industry competitiveness is positive, negative, or conditional on complementary policies (e.g., credit access, infrastructure).

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic industry equilibrium model incorporating infant industry learning curves, trade costs, and credit constraints, calibrated to data from Thailand and Ghana — Provides a structural framework to disentangle the mechanisms through which free trade policies may strengthen or weaken infant industries, and to simulate counterfactual policy scenarios (e.g., gradual vs. sudden liberalization).

qualifier.temporal: during the early stages of trade liberalization (e.g., 1990s–2010s)
qualifier.geographic: in developing economies in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa
